title: Containment flow guards and capacity recovery automation for hosted GPU exhaustion incidents
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Summary: During a hosted API capacity event on 2026-02-28 we observed sustained GPU exhaustion in two EMEA pools that caused multi-minute queue buildup, aggressive throttling at the admission layer, and a cascade of retries from some high-concurrency tenants. This ticket captures the prioritized follow-ups: implement containment flow-guards (soft caps + progressive admission), automate emergency capacity priming (fast warm-up of idle reserved nodes), and add an automated recovery orchestration that reduces human toil and blast radius for future events.

Root cause hypothesis: A simultaneous traffic spike from a small number of high-concurrency tenants (3 tenants) with large context windows drove continuous full-GPU occupancy. Autoscaling did not trigger quickly enough because the current scale-up cooldown and instance warm-up window are optimized for gradual growth, not sudden bursts. Admission gating then imposed a single global throttle which resulted in request pile-up and retry storms.

Goals and acceptance criteria:
- Containment flow-guards in front of the GPU scheduler to limit per-tenant concurrency and apply measurable backpressure without global hard-fails (AC1: no single tenant can saturate a pool beyond configured window; AC2: mean queue wait time during a similar synthetic spike is < 3s).
- Emergency capacity priming automation to rapidly bring standby GPUs into active pool within 60s for EMEA and US regions (AC3: reduce time-to-available-GPU by >= 70% in test).
- Recovery orchestration runbook and playbook codified with automated remediation steps (AC4: runbook drills executed with SREs and product on-call; playbook reduces manual steps from 12->3).

Planned deliverables:
1) Admission layer changes: implement progressive admission windows (soft cap -> degrade -> hard cap) and per-tenant concurrency tokens. Includes metrics (tokens_granted, tokens_rejected, per_tenant_concurrency).
2) Fast priming: implement a warm-start job that can trigger GPU VM/container warm-up and prefetch model weights onto cache for a target pool. Integrate with capacity leader election to avoid thundering herd.
3) Recovery orchestrator: a serverless workflow that runs prechecks, triggers priming, applies temporary priority rules, and notifies on-call.
4) Dashboards & alerts: new Grafana panels for per-tenant concurrency, admission window saturation, priming job latency and success rate.
5) Runbook update: step-by-step automated and manual escalation paths plus post-incident checklist.

Technical tradeoffs discussed:
- Per-tenant limits reduce tail latency for others but may frustrate heavy-paying customers; mitigation: provide override/whitelisting via Dedicated capacity or SLA contracts.
- Aggressive priming increases cost if misfired; mitigation: limit automatic priming to defined traffic heuristics and a budgeted pool.

Rollout plan:
- Stage 1 (canary): implement admission windows and metrics in staging and roll to one non-critical EMEA pool; run synthetic spike tests.
- Stage 2: add priming automation behind feature flag, test across two pools (one EMEA, one US) with controlled spikes.
- Stage 3: enable recovery orchestrator and simulate full playbook in game-day.
- Stage 4: global rollout and policy defaults.

Monitoring and telemetry:
- Grafana: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/abc123/gpu-pools-new-view and https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/priming/priming-jobs
- Incident timeline & logs: https://logs.redwood.ai/incident/2026-02-28-gpu-exhaustion
- PRD and design notes: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RUNTIME/Containment+and+Priming+PRD

Notes on backwards compatibility: admission window changes are implemented as a gateway layer flaggable per-pool to avoid affecting Dedicated pools until we validate behavior. Priming APIs expose safe defaults and require an allowlist for pools accessible by private deployments.

Security & compliance: no customer data will be replicated; priming fetches models already present in our catalog and follows existing KMS flow. Ensure audit logs capture priming triggers for post-mortem.
